fixes.explanation: Rest is a nice thought, friend, and I'd take a nap right now. But the Teacher says “…a time to be silent and a time to speak…” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Silent is paired with speak, its opposite. Rest just wasn't invited to this pair.

That fits the first half of the passage, friend, where times keep trading places. But verse 14 says something else about God's work. “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). The word the Teacher uses is endures.

Look again, friend, because it does say that. The Teacher says, “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Taken from it is right there in the verse. So the answer is true.

Rest sounds lovely, friend, and my apron strings agree. But the verse gives a different reason. It says, “God does it so that they should fear Him.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). That's the reason the Teacher states.

Kings do make a good guess, friend, but they never show up in that verse. The Teacher says, “God does it so that they should fear Him.” (Ecclesiastes 3:14). That's the reason he gives. Rulers aren't mentioned in it.

True, baker. The last line says, “…for God will call to account what has passed.” (Ecclesiastes 3:15). The Teacher just says it plain, no extra frosting. Sometimes the short sentences are the ones that make you set your spatula down.

Check that last verse again, friend, because it's sitting right there. The Teacher says, “…for God will call to account what has passed.” (Ecclesiastes 3:15). I've reread a verse three times before and found the answer waiting every time. So the answer is true.
